questions.question: A periodically reviewed single-item inventory system with a positive lead time uses a $(T,s,S)$ policy with reorder level $s$, order-up-to level $S>s$ and a clock of $T$ periods. When is an order that raises the inventory position to $S$ placed?
options: At the end of a period in which the position is at or below $s$ and at least $T$ periods have passed since the last order.
At the end of a period in which the position equals $s$ exactly, or once $T$ periods have passed since the last order.
At the end of the first period in which the position is at or below $s$ or $T$ periods have passed since the last order.
At the end of the first period in which the inventory level is at or below $s$ or $T$ periods have passed since the last order.

questions.question: A $(T,s,S)$ policy adds a level trigger (order when the inventory position is at or below $s$) to a $(T,S)$ policy, which orders up to $S$ once every $T$ periods. Which drawback of the $(T,S)$ policy does the level trigger remove?
options: It waits for the next scheduled order even when the position has already fallen far below what is needed.
It orders the same fixed quantity every $T$ periods, whatever the demand since the last order has been.
Its cost recursion refers to itself after a period with zero demand, so the self-term must be isolated.
Its replenishment cycles can last arbitrarily long when demand stays low for many periods in a row.

questions.question: Under a $(T,s,S)$ policy the expected cost until the next order satisfies $V(n,s,x)=L(x)+\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,s,x-D)]$ for $x>s$, $n>0$, and $V(n,s,x)=K$ otherwise, with running cost $L$ and order cost $K$. Which running and stopping cost turn this recursion into the expected number of periods $T(n,s,x)$ until the next order?

A $(T,s,S)$ policy with $T=5$, $s=2$ and $S=4$ faces i.i.d. period demands on $\{0,1,2\}$, each value having positive probability. Which statement about the length of a replenishment cycle, from one order to the next, is correct?
options: The cycle always lasts exactly $5$ periods.
The cycle never lasts longer than $5$ periods.
The cycle lasts at most $S-s=2$ periods.
The cycle can exceed $5$ periods if demand stays at $0$.

questions.question: Consider a $(T,s,S)$ policy with i.i.d. period demands, and keep the clock length $T$ and the order-up-to level $S$ fixed. As the reorder level $s\to-\infty$, the long-run average cost converges to that of which policy?
options: The $(s,S)$ policy with the same order-up-to level $S$.
The base-stock policy with order-up-to level $S$.
The $(T,S)$ policy with the same $T$ and $S$.
None: the average cost grows without bound.

questions.question: Under a $(T,s,S)$ policy with $T=4$, $s=2$ and $S=7$, an order at the end of period $0$ raised the inventory position to $7$. The demands in periods $1$ to $5$ are $1,2,0,1,3$. When is the next order placed, and how many units does it order?

A $(T,s,S)$ policy has $T=4$, $s=1$, $S=6$, order cost $K=8$ and running cost $L(0)=5$ at position $0$. With two periods left on the clock, the inventory position has just dropped to $x=0$. What is the expected cost until and including the next order, $V(2,1,0)$?

A $(T,s,S)$ policy with $T=1$, $s=1$ and $S=3$ controls a system with holding cost $h=1$ per unit per period, lead time $1$, order cost $K=6$ and running cost $L(3)=2$ at position $3$. What is its long-run average cost per period?

Under a $(T,s,S)$ policy with $T=3$, $s=1$ and $S=5$, the inventory position is $5$ at the start of period $1$, just after an order. The demands in periods $1$ to $8$ are $0,1,3,2,2,1,0,1$. At the end of which periods are orders placed?

For a $(T,s,S)$ policy with $T=3$, $s=1$ and $S=5$, the cost recursion stops in a state $(n,x)$, with $n$ periods left on the clock and position $x$, and returns the order cost $K$. Which of these states is not a stopping state and still needs a recursion step?

The $(s,S)$ cost recursion needs a division by $1-f_0$, where $f_0=\mathbb{P}(D=0)$, because a period without demand leaves its state unchanged. Why does the $(T,s,S)$ recursion $V(n,s,x)=L(x)+\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,s,x-D)]$ for $x>s$, $n>0$ need no such division, even when $f_0>0$?
options: Zero demand leads from $(n,x)$ to $(n-1,x)$, a different state, so the recursion never calls itself.
The running cost $L(x)$ already contains the factor $\frac{1}{1-f_0}$ through the lead-time demand.
A period with zero demand costs nothing, so it can simply be left out of the recursion.
The factor $\frac{1}{1-f_0}$ is still there but cancels in the ratio $V(T,s,S)/T(T,s,S)$.

questions.question: For a $(T,s,S)$ policy with i.i.d. period demands, the long-run average cost is $V(T,s,S)/T(T,s,S)$: the expected cost of one replenishment cycle divided by its expected length. Why is this ratio the right quantity?
options: Every cycle lasts exactly $T$ periods, so the expected cycle cost is spread evenly over the clock.
Every cycle starts in state $(n,x)=(T,S)$ and demands are i.i.d., so cycles are i.i.d. and renewal reward applies.
The inventory position is uniform on $\{s+1,\dots,S\}$, so each period has the same expected cost.
The ratio of the two expectations equals the expected cost per period averaged over single cycles.

questions.question: A $(T,s,S)$ policy faces i.i.d. period demands with $0<\mathbb{P}(D=0)<1$. With $s<S$ fixed, its long-run average cost tends to that of the $(s,S)$ policy as $T\to\infty$. What is the reason?
options: Once $T>S-s$, the level trigger fires before the clock for every possible demand sequence.
The order cost $K$ is spread over $T$ periods, so it vanishes from the average cost.
The expected cycle length grows without bound, so only the running cost remains.
For large $T$ the position reaches $\{x\leq s\}$ before the clock runs out with probability close to $1$.

questions.question: A $(T,s,S)$ policy has $T=2$, $s=0$, $S=2$ and order cost $K=8$. Period demand $D$ has $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=\mathbb{P}(D=2)=\tfrac{1}{4}$, and the running costs are $L(0)=3$, $L(1)=\tfrac{3}{2}$, $L(2)=\tfrac{5}{4}$. What is the expected cost $V(2,0,2)$ of one cycle, including its order?

A $(T,s,S)$ policy has $T=3$, $s=0$ and $S=3$, and period demands are i.i.d. and uniform on $\{0,1,2\}$. A cycle starts at position $3$. What is the probability that the level trigger ends the cycle before the clock fires, that is, that the cycle lasts fewer than $3$ periods?

A grid search over $(T,s,S)$ policies reports, per candidate, the expected cycle cost $V$ and the expected cycle length $\tau$: $(2,1,6)$: $V=9.0$, $\tau=1.8$; $(3,1,6)$: $V=11.5$, $\tau=2.5$; $(4,1,6)$: $V=14.4$, $\tau=2.9$; $(4,0,7)$: $V=16.0$, $\tau=3.4$. Which candidate has the lowest long-run average cost?

For fixed integers $s<S$ and a fixed clock length $T$, compare the long-run average cost of the $(T,s,S)$ policy with those of the $(s,S)$ policy and the $(T,S)$ policy with the same parameters and the same demand and cost data. Which statement is correct?
options: It is never above the smaller of the two, since an extra trigger can only help.
It always lies between the two, since the policy mixes their two triggers.
It can exceed the $(s,S)$ cost but never the $(T,S)$ cost, since the level trigger only acts at low positions.
It can exceed both, since a trigger can end cycles that were cheap to continue.

questions.question: Under an $(s,S)$ policy with integers $s<S$, every order raises the inventory position from at most $s$ to $S$, so each order is at least $S-s$ units. Under a $(T,s,S)$ policy with the same $s$ and $S$, which statement about the order sizes is correct?
options: An order placed by the clock can be smaller than $S-s$, since the position may still be above $s$.
Every order is still at least $S-s$, since every order raises the position up to $S$.
Every order is exactly $S-s$, since an order raises the position from $s$ to $S$.
Clock orders are always larger than level orders, since more periods of demand have passed.

questions.question: A $(T,s,S)$ policy has $T=3$, $s=0$ and $S=2$, and period demands are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=\mathbb{P}(D=1)=\tfrac{1}{2}$. What is the expected cycle length $T(3,0,2)$, the expected number of periods from one order to the next?

A $(T,s,S)$ policy has $s=2$ and $S=8$, and period demands are i.i.d. and uniform on $\{1,2,3\}$, so every period has demand at least $1$. What is the smallest clock length $T$ for which this policy places exactly the same orders as the $(s,S)$ policy for every possible demand sequence?
